rows.question: Trace an external HTTPS request from the cluster edge to a ready application Pod and name the Kubernetes abstractions involved.
rows.answer: An external HTTPS request in a Kubernetes cluster typically follows this flow: 1. The request first hits the Ingress, which exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services within the cluster. The Ingress resource defines rules for traffic routing, such as SSL/TLS termination and name-based virtual hosting. 2. An Ingress Controller is responsible for fulfilling the Ingress resource, usually by configuring a load balancer or edge router to handle the traffic. The Ingress Controller ensures that the traffic is directed according to the rules specified in the Ingress. 3. Once the request is routed by the Ingress, it reaches the appropriate Service. The Service provides a stable endpoint for accessing the Pods and can be configured with traffic policies to control routing to healthy backends. 4. The Service routes the request to one of the Pods, which are the actual endpoints serving the application. Pods can be configured with readiness and liveness probes to ensure they are ready to receive traffic and are functioning correctly. If a readiness probe fails, the Pod will not receive traffic from the Service.

rows.question: Use the probability and statistics PDF as the authority: explain how kube-scheduler scores candidate nodes.
rows.answer: The active scoring rules used by kube-scheduler to evaluate candidate nodes after the filtering step are configured through Scheduling Policies and Scheduling Profiles. Scheduling Policies allow configuration of Priorities for scoring, while Scheduling Profiles allow configuration of Plugins that implement different scheduling stages, including Score.

rows.question: Only frontend Pods may call the payments Pods on TCP 8443, and payments must not initiate other egress. What policy model expresses this?
rows.answer:
To express the policy model where only frontend Pods may call the payments Pods on TCP 8443, and payments Pods must not initiate other egress, you would need two NetworkPolicies: 
1. An ingress policy on the payments Pods that allows traffic from frontend Pods on TCP 8443. 
2. An egress policy on the payments Pods that denies all egress traffic. 

The ingress policy would specify the frontend Pods as the source and TCP 8443 as the allowed port. The egress policy would be a default deny all egress policy, ensuring no outgoing connections are allowed from the payments Pods.

This policy has no effect on isolation for ingress to any pod.Default deny all ingress and all egress trafficYou can create a "default" policy for a namespace which prevents all ingress AND egress traffic by creating the following NetworkPolicy in that namespace.service/networking/network-policy-default-deny-all.yaml --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: default-deny-all spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any other NetworkPolicy will not be

[Evidence source: concepts__services-networking__network-policies.html]
additively.Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.The NetworkPolicy resourceSee the NetworkPolicy reference for a full definition of the resource.An example NetworkPolicy might look like this:service/networking/networkpolicy.yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: test-network-policy namespace: default spec: podSelector: matchLabels: role: db policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress ingress: - from: - ipBlock: cidr: 172.17.0.0/16 except: - 172.17.1.0/24 - namespaceS

rows.question: If I edit a ConfigMap used by running Pods, when will the application observe the new value, and what differs between a mounted file and an environment variable?
rows.answer: When a ConfigMap is updated, the application will observe the new value at different times depending on how the ConfigMap is used. For a ConfigMap consumed as a mounted file, the kubelet periodically checks if the ConfigMap is fresh and updates the projected keys automatically. The delay for observing the new value can be as long as the kubelet sync period plus the cache propagation delay, which depends on the cache type used [concepts__configuration__configmap.html]. In contrast, if the ConfigMap is used as an environment variable, the application will not observe the new value until the Pod is restarted, as environment variables are not updated automatically [concepts__configuration__configmap.html].

rows.ground_truth: ConfigMap data projected into a mounted volume is updated eventually by kubelet synchronization, although an application may need to reread the file. Values injected as environment variables are fixed when the container starts, so existing containers require a restart or rollout to receive the changed value.

ragas_metrics.answer: When a ConfigMap is updated, the application will observe the new value at different times depending on how the ConfigMap is used. For a ConfigMap consumed as a mounted file, the kubelet periodically checks if the ConfigMap is fresh and updates the projected keys automatically. The delay for observing the new value can be as long as the kubelet sync period plus the cache propagation delay, which depends on the cache type used [concepts__configuration__configmap.html]. In contrast, if the ConfigMap is used as an environment variable, the application will not observe the new value until the Pod is restarted, as environment variables are not updated automatically [concepts__configuration__configmap.html].

ragas_metrics.ground_truth: ConfigMap data projected into a mounted volume is updated eventually by kubelet synchronization, although an application may need to reread the file. Values injected as environment variables are fixed when the container starts, so existing containers require a restart or rollout to receive the changed value.
